movements.name: American Modernism
movements.summary: European avant-garde form, carried by émigrés and adopted by American business, stripped of ideology and turned into a tool for clarity and impact.

principles.name: Form without the manifesto
principles.idea: The avant-garde toolkit of asymmetry, sans-serif, photomontage and primary colour is adopted for clarity and impact, not as a social programme.
principles.example: Lester Beall, Rural Electrification Administration posters, 1937

principles.name: The photograph as raw material
principles.idea: Photographs are cropped hard, bled, scaled against each other and made to converse with type rather than framed as pictures.
principles.example: Alexey Brodovitch, Harper's Bazaar spreads, from 1934

principles.name: White space is active
principles.idea: Emptiness is the frame that makes the one element on the page loud.

principles.name: Information as architecture
principles.idea: Large bodies of facts are organised by signs, tabs, grids and colour so a reader can navigate rather than merely read.
principles.example: Ladislav Sutnar and Knud Lönberg-Holm, Catalog Design, 1944

principles.name: Enlightened patronage
principles.idea: A company commissions art rather than advertising and lets the artist sign it, buying an image of intelligence.
principles.example: Container Corporation of America, Great Ideas of Western Man campaign, from 1950

movements.name: New York School
aka: New York School of graphic design
movements.summary: American-born designers made the émigré toolkit witty and argumentative: one visual idea, often a pun, carrying the whole message.

principles.name: The idea is the design
principles.idea: A single compressible concept, visual or verbal, carries the communication; style only serves it.
principles.example: Paul Rand, Eye-Bee-M poster for IBM, 1981

principles.name: Wit and the visual pun
principles.idea: Juxtaposition and double meaning make the viewer complete the message and remember it.
principles.example: Doyle Dane Bernbach (art director Helmut Krone), Think Small Volkswagen ad, 1959

principles.name: Word and image as one
principles.idea: Copy and picture are conceived together, often by art director and copywriter in the same room.
principles.example: George Lois, Muhammad Ali as Saint Sebastian, Esquire cover, 1968

principles.name: The handmade inside the modern
principles.idea: Collage, torn paper, brush lettering and childlike drawing loosen an otherwise spare modern page.
principles.example: Saul Bass, The Man with the Golden Arm poster, 1955

principles.name: Simplify to the symbol
principles.idea: Reduce a complex organisation or product to one memorable sign.

keyWorks.title: The Man with the Golden Arm

movements.name: Midcentury Modern
movements.summary: Postwar American design where new materials, furniture makers' patronage and a playful West Coast spirit joined furniture, film, exhibition and graphics.

principles.name: The material leads the form
principles.idea: New processes produce new shapes, and the object shows how it was made.
principles.example: Charles and Ray Eames, LCW moulded-plywood chair, 1946

principles.name: Design within constraints
principles.idea: The designer's skill is recognising every constraint and working within it with enthusiasm.
principles.example: Charles and Ray Eames, Eames House from off-the-shelf industrial parts, 1949

principles.name: One discipline across media
principles.idea: The same office makes chairs, toys, films, exhibitions and graphics with one sensibility.
principles.example: Charles and Ray Eames, Mathematica exhibition, 1961

principles.name: Play as method
principles.idea: Toys, games and collections are treated as serious design research.
principles.example: Charles and Ray Eames, House of Cards, 1952

principles.name: Explain with film and exhibition
principles.idea: Complex ideas are taught through multi-screen film and walk-through shows.
principles.example: Charles and Ray Eames, Glimpses of the USA, Moscow, 1959

movements.name: Corporate Identity
movements.summary: National and multinational companies adopted a simple symbol plus a written standards manual, so one visual system could run across everything they touched.

principles.name: The mark as irreducible symbol
principles.idea: A simple, often abstract mark can stand for a vast and complex company.

principles.name: The standards manual
principles.idea: Rules for colour, type, spacing and applications are written down so thousands of people apply the identity consistently.
principles.example: Saul Bass, Bell System identity manual, 1969

principles.name: Total design
principles.idea: Graphics, products, architecture and environments speak one language under one design director.
principles.example: IBM design programme under Eliot Noyes with Paul Rand, from 1956

principles.name: Longevity over fashion
principles.idea: A mark is designed for decades, not for a campaign.
principles.example: Chermayeff & Geismar, Mobil wordmark with the red o, 1964

movements.name: American Systems Modernism
movements.summary: Swiss-trained rationalism industrialised in America: Helvetica, modular grids and standards manuals for corporations, transit systems and the federal government.

principles.name: The grid as operating system
principles.idea: Every piece is built on a modular grid so many hands produce consistent results.
principles.example: Massimo Vignelli, National Park Service Unigrid, 1977

principles.name: A limited typeface set
principles.idea: A handful of faces, used with discipline, is enough for almost anything.
principles.example: Unimark (Vignelli and Bob Noorda), NYCTA Graphics Standards Manual in Helvetica, 1970

principles.name: Information over expression
principles.idea: The designer is a problem-solver serving the user, not an artist expressing a self.
principles.example: AIGA and US Department of Transportation, Symbol Signs, 1974

principles.name: Abstraction for legibility
principles.idea: A diagram beats a map when the user needs connections more than geography.
principles.example: Massimo Vignelli, New York City Subway diagram, 1972

principles.name: Design as public service
principles.idea: Government should communicate as well as the best corporations.
principles.example: Danne & Blackburn, NASA logotype and graphics standards manual, 1975

keyWorks.title: New York City Transit Authority Graphics Standards Manual

movements.name: Push Pin Style
movements.summary: Illustrator-designers who answered modernist correctness by raiding Victoriana, Art Nouveau, Deco and comics, with wit, bulbous line and flat colour.

principles.name: History as a toolbox
principles.idea: Any past style can be revived, reinterpreted and combined to serve a new idea.

principles.name: Illustration is design
principles.idea: Drawing, type and concept are made by one hand as one object.
principles.example: Seymour Chwast, End Bad Breath poster, 1967

principles.name: Wit over neutrality
principles.idea: Humour and irony replace modernist objectivity.
principles.example: Push Pin Studios, The Push Pin Graphic, from 1957

principles.name: Display type as personality
principles.idea: Custom phototype display faces give every job its own voice.
principles.example: Seymour Chwast, Artone typeface for Photo-Lettering, 1964

movements.name: Expressive Typography (US)
movements.summary: Phototype freed display letters from metal, and New York art directors kerned, overlapped and scaled words until the word itself became the image.

principles.name: Typography as image
principles.idea: The word becomes the picture; meaning is expressed through the form of the letters.

principles.name: Tight, touching type
principles.idea: Phototype lets letters be kerned until they touch and overlap, forming new shapes.
principles.example: Herb Lubalin, Avant Garde magazine logotype, 1968

principles.name: Ligatures as expression
principles.idea: Alternates and ligatures are designed as the face's personality, not as exceptions.
principles.example: Herb Lubalin and Tom Carnase, ITC Avant Garde Gothic, 1970

principles.name: Type as architecture
principles.idea: Lettering at environmental scale turns a wall into a typographic composition.

figures.name: Alexey Brodovitch
figures.summary: Harper's Bazaar art director 1934–58 who made the magazine a cinematic sequence of bled photographs and white space, and taught a generation of photographers.

principles.name: Cinematic pacing
principles.idea: A magazine is an edited sequence; spreads rhyme, accelerate and pause like film.

principles.name: Type takes the shape of the picture
principles.idea: Text blocks are cut to echo the forms in the photograph.

principles.name: Shock value on every page
principles.idea: Each page must surprise; never show the reader what they have seen before.

keyWorks.title: Observations (with Richard Avedon and Truman Capote)

figures.name: Herbert Matter
figures.summary: Swiss photomontage pioneer who brought scale collision to America and built Knoll's identity almost entirely out of how its furniture was photographed.

principles.name: Scale collision
principles.idea: A huge close-up beside a tiny figure makes the image deep before a word is read.

principles.name: The product as abstract sculpture
principles.idea: Furniture is photographed as form, shadow and line with almost no copy.

principles.name: One sign for a whole system
principles.idea: A single monogram applied to everything from vehicles to timetables.

figures.name: Lester Beall
figures.summary: Among the first American-born modernists; his Rural Electrification posters turned Constructivist arrows and stripes into a public American language.

principles.name: Graphic signs over illustration
principles.idea: Arrows, stripes and flat flags persuade more directly than a painted scene.

principles.name: Photomontage for the common good
principles.idea: Documentary photographs of real people, cut out against flat colour, sell a public programme.

principles.name: Codify the mark
principles.idea: An identity is written into a standards manual so it outlives its designer.

figures.name: Ladislav Sutnar
figures.summary: Czech avant-gardist stranded in New York in 1939 who, at Sweet's Catalog Service, invented much of modern information design and navigation.

principles.name: Visual flow
principles.idea: A document is designed as a path, leading the eye from general to specific by size, colour, position and sign.

principles.name: Function, not decoration
principles.idea: Every bar, tab and circled numeral has a navigational job.

principles.name: Punctuation as structure
principles.idea: Brackets, rules and numerals organise information; he is credited with parenthesised area codes.

keyWorks.title: Package Design: The Force of Visual Selling

figures.name: Will Burtin
figures.summary: German émigré who art-directed Fortune and then gave science a human scale, most famously in the walk-in model The Cell.

principles.name: Make the invisible visible
principles.idea: Scientific processes are given physical form at human scale.

principles.name: Teach under pressure
principles.idea: Instruction must work for a frightened novice in a moving aircraft.

principles.name: Integration
principles.idea: Art, science and technology are one design problem.

figures.name: Alvin Lustig
figures.role: Book designer, graphic and interior designer
figures.summary: Made the New Directions paperback a site of modern art with abstract, symbolic jackets, and argued the designer should be a generalist.

principles.name: Symbol, not illustration
principles.idea: A jacket evokes the spirit of the text with an abstract sign rather than depicting a scene.

principles.name: The designer as total designer
principles.idea: One designer moves across books, interiors, furniture and type.

principles.name: Modern art as vernacular
principles.idea: Lessons from Miró, Klee and Surrealism reach a mass audience on a cheap cover.
principles.example: A Streetcar Named Desire jacket, New Directions, 1947

figures.name: Paul Rand
figures.summary: Gave American design its theory in Thoughts on Design and its corporate face in IBM, Westinghouse, UPS and ABC: the idea first, delivered with play.

principles.name: The idea
principles.idea: Design starts from a concept that reconciles the client's problem with a visual form; without it everything is decoration.

principles.name: Play
principles.idea: Design is a game with rules; wit and surprise make a problem solvable and memorable.
principles.example: Essay Design and the Play Instinct, in Kepes's Education of Vision, 1965

principles.name: Form and content
principles.idea: Content is what is said, form is how; good design fuses them and makes the commonplace strange.

principles.name: Simplicity and restraint
principles.idea: A mark must survive blurring, reduction and misuse.

figures.name: Saul Bass
figures.summary: Turned film titles into a prologue and posters into one cut-paper symbol, then built some of America's longest-lived corporate marks.

principles.name: Symbolize and summarize
principles.idea: Reduce a whole film or company to one graphic sign used everywhere.
principles.example: The Man with the Golden Arm poster and titles, 1955

principles.name: Titles as prologue
principles.idea: The credit sequence sets mood and theme before the first scene.

principles.name: Making the ordinary extraordinary
principles.idea: Familiar things are shown in an unfamiliar way.
principles.example: Walk on the Wild Side title sequence, 1962

principles.name: Marks that outlive companies
principles.idea: Simple symbolic logos designed to last decades.

keyWorks.title: The Man with the Golden Arm

figures.name: Bradbury Thompson
figures.summary: Turned a paper company's promotion, Westvaco Inspirations, into a laboratory where printing's own process colours and plates became the image.

principles.name: Process as image
principles.idea: Separations, halftone dots and printing plates become the illustration.

principles.name: Old and new together
principles.idea: Antique engravings sit beside modern type and colour.

principles.name: Reform the alphabet
principles.idea: Question the two-case system with one form per letter.

principles.name: Read as spoken
principles.idea: Break lines by phrase and cadence, not by measure.

figures.name: Cipe Pineles
figures.summary: First woman to art-direct major American mass-market magazines; at Seventeen and Charm she brought fine artists and real women's lives onto the page.

principles.name: Fine art in mass media
principles.idea: Commission serious painters, not illustrators, to interpret fiction.
principles.example: Seventeen, with art by Ben Shahn, Ad Reinhardt and Andy Warhol, 1947–50

principles.name: Design for the reader's real life
principles.idea: Fashion shown in offices and streets for women who work.

principles.name: The hand as voice
principles.idea: Painted, hand-lettered illustration warms photographic glamour.
principles.example: Leave Me Alone with the Recipes, made 1940s, published 2017

figures.name: George Lois
figures.summary: Creative Revolution provocateur whose Esquire covers made a single staged image into an editorial argument.

principles.name: The Big Idea
principles.idea: One provocative, instantly graspable concept beats a hundred well-made layouts.
principles.example: Muhammad Ali as Saint Sebastian, Esquire, April 1968

principles.name: Image as editorial
principles.idea: A cover is an argument, not a decoration.
principles.example: Andy Warhol in a Campbell's soup can, Esquire, May 1969

principles.name: Speak in the audience's voice
principles.idea: Put the slogan in the mouth of the viewer.

figures.name: Charles and Ray Eames
figures.role: Designers: furniture, film, exhibition, architecture (the Eames Office)
figures.summary: Husband-and-wife office (Charles 1907–1978, Ray 1912–1988) that made furniture, toys, films and exhibitions one discipline of learning by doing.

principles.name: Learning by doing
principles.idea: Prototype endlessly; the model is the argument.
principles.example: Moulded plywood experiments leading to the LCW chair, 1946

principles.name: The best for the most for the least
principles.idea: Industrial production serves good design for ordinary people.

principles.name: Powers of scale
principles.idea: Understand a system by seeing it at every scale.

principles.name: Design depends on constraints
principles.idea: Recognise as many constraints as possible and work within them with enthusiasm.

keyWorks.title: Mathematica: A World of Numbers... and Beyond

figures.name: Louis Danziger
figures.summary: Los Angeles modernist, taught by Lustig and Brodovitch, who brought Constructivist structure to American advertising and then taught design history for decades.

principles.name: Constructivist form for ordinary products
principles.idea: Diagonals, photography and type as structure, applied to everyday advertising.

principles.name: Clarity as intelligence
principles.idea: Respect the reader enough to say one thing.
principles.example: Container Corporation of America print ad, 1958

principles.name: Teach the history
principles.idea: A designer's longest-lasting work can be teaching where solutions came from.

keyWorks.title: New York School exhibition poster, LACMA

figures.name: Chermayeff & Geismar
figures.role: Identity design firm (Chermayeff & Geismar & Haviv since 2013)
figures.summary: Ivan Chermayeff and Tom Geismar's firm, founded with Robert Brownjohn, which made the abstract corporate symbol American: Chase, Mobil, NBC, PBS.

principles.name: Memorable, appropriate, simple
principles.idea: A mark must be all three; abstraction is allowed when the company cannot be pictured.

principles.name: Type as the mark
principles.idea: A wordmark with one distinctive gesture.

principles.name: Refresh, don't replace
principles.idea: Evolve heritage marks rather than discard their equity.
principles.example: NBC peacock reduced to six feathers, 1986

figures.name: Ivan Chermayeff
figures.summary: Co-founder of Chermayeff & Geismar whose identity rigour sat alongside hundreds of loose, witty collage posters and children's books.

principles.name: Collage as found wit
principles.idea: Scraps of everyday material assembled into a portrait or scene.
principles.example: Collage posters for Mobil-sponsored public television arts programming, 1970s–80s

principles.name: Words that move
principles.idea: Typography should act out its meaning.
principles.example: Watching Words Move, with Brownjohn and Geismar, 1959

principles.name: Teach shapes first
principles.idea: Basic forms are the first vocabulary of seeing.

figures.name: Pentagram
figures.summary: Partnership of equals founded in London in 1972; its New York office (1978) became the main heir of New York School wit in identity design.

principles.name: A partnership of designers
principles.idea: Each partner leads their own clients and team; profits are shared equally.

principles.name: The idea, again
principles.idea: Wit and concept carried from Fletcher/Forbes/Gill into identity work.

principles.name: Identity as voice
principles.idea: Typography and tone carry a brand as much as a logo does.
principles.example: Michael Bierut, Saks Fifth Avenue identity, 2007

figures.name: Unimark International
figures.role: International design firm (Chicago, New York, Milan)
figures.summary: Design firm run like a corporation, briefly the world's largest, that sold grids, Helvetica and manuals instead of artistic personality.

principles.name: Design as a business discipline
principles.idea: Replace the designer-as-artist with standardised, repeatable method.
principles.example: Unimark's corporate structure and client manuals, from 1965

principles.name: Helvetica and the grid as defaults
principles.idea: A neutral typeface on a modular grid lets many hands stay consistent.

principles.name: Identity across every touchpoint
principles.idea: One system governs aircraft, tickets, signs and stationery.

keyWorks.title: New York City Transit Authority Graphics Standards Manual

figures.name: Massimo Vignelli
figures.summary: Italian rationalist who systematised American public and corporate design; his Canon is semantics, syntactics, pragmatics and a handful of typefaces.

principles.name: Semantics, syntactics, pragmatics
principles.idea: Find the meaning, give it a consistent grammar of grid, type and colour, then make sure it is understood.

principles.name: Discipline and appropriateness
principles.idea: Self-imposed rules applied to every detail; the solution fits the problem, not a style.

principles.name: Ambiguity, used sparingly
principles.idea: A plurality of meanings can enrich a design, but contradiction usually signals loss of control.

principles.name: A limited typeface set
principles.idea: Garamond, Bodoni, Century Expanded and Helvetica, plus a few more, are enough; it is not the type but what you do with it.

keyWorks.title: NYCTA Graphics Standards Manual (with Bob Noorda)

figures.name: Lella Vignelli
figures.role: Architect, interior and product designer, studio CEO
figures.summary: Architect and long-under-credited co-founder of Unimark and Vignelli Associates, who led its three-dimensional work and ran the practice.

principles.name: Design is one, in three dimensions
principles.idea: The same discipline governs a plate, a chair and a showroom.

principles.name: Sprezzatura
principles.idea: Rigour that looks effortless.

principles.name: The office as a design
principles.idea: Running the practice, its clients, money and people, is part of the work.

figures.name: Milton Glaser
figures.summary: Push Pin co-founder, New York magazine co-founder and author of I♥NY, who argued that style is a means and just enough is more.

principles.name: Just enough is more
principles.idea: Neither modernist reduction nor ornament by reflex, just enough to make the idea live.

principles.name: Style is not to be trusted
principles.idea: Any style can serve an idea; none is a virtue in itself.

principles.name: Design for civic good
principles.idea: A mark can change how people feel about a place.

figures.name: Seymour Chwast
figures.summary: Push Pin co-founder whose thick, comic line, woodcut sources and display faces made protest and commerce funny.

principles.name: Protest through humour
principles.idea: The anti-war poster as a cartoon can carry more weight than a photograph.

principles.name: The vernacular as source
principles.idea: Woodcut, comics and naive drawing are legitimate design languages.

principles.name: Type that draws
principles.idea: Display faces are illustrations in alphabet form.

figures.name: Herb Lubalin
figures.summary: Master of 'typographics' who used phototype to make words into images, from Mother & Child to Avant Garde, ITC and U&lc.

principles.name: Typographics
principles.idea: Type is not set but designed into an image of its own meaning.

principles.name: The logotype as editorial
principles.idea: A masthead can be a manifesto for the magazine it heads.

principles.name: Promote type by showing it off
principles.idea: A type catalogue disguised as a lively magazine sells faces by using them.

keyWorks.title: ITC Avant Garde Gothic (with Tom Carnase)

figures.name: Paula Scher
figures.summary: From CBS Records covers to Pentagram's Public Theater identity, she spoke new things in the borrowed grammar of Constructivism and wood type.

principles.name: Historical vocabulary, not historical copy
principles.idea: Borrow the grammar of Constructivism or Deco and say something new with it.
principles.example: The Best of Jazz poster, CBS Records, 1979

principles.name: Parody as homage
principles.idea: Reprise a classic so precisely the reference becomes the message.

principles.name: Type as the street
principles.idea: Loud, mixed wood type that feels like the city an institution lives in.

keyWorks.title: Bring in 'da Noise, Bring in 'da Funk

events.label: Brodovitch joins Harper's Bazaar
events.note: European avant-garde layout enters the American mass-market magazine.

events.label: New Bauhaus opens in Chicago
events.note: Moholy-Nagy transplants Bauhaus teaching to the US, backed by Walter Paepcke's circle.

events.label: MoMA's Bauhaus 1919–1928 exhibition
events.note: Gives émigré modernism institutional standing in America.

events.label: CCA Great Ideas of Western Man
events.note: Container Corporation's campaign proves enlightened corporate patronage of designers.

events.label: International Design Conference in Aspen
events.note: Walter Paepcke's conference links designers and business leaders for decades.

events.label: CBS eye
events.note: William Golden shows a single symbol can carry a brand on television.

events.label: The Man with the Golden Arm titles
events.note: Saul Bass makes the film title sequence a designed prologue.

events.label: IBM logo and design programme
events.note: Rand's mark and Eliot Noyes's total design programme set the template for corporate identity.

events.label: Think Small (Volkswagen)
events.note: DDB's ad crowns the Creative Revolution's idea-first, art-director-plus-copywriter method.

events.label: Chase Manhattan octagon
events.note: One of the first purely abstract American corporate symbols.

events.label: Unimark International founded
events.note: Systems modernism is industrialised as a corporate design firm.

events.label: NYCTA Graphics Standards Manual
events.note: Vignelli and Noorda's manual makes Helvetica the voice of the New York subway.

events.label: International Typeface Corporation founded
events.note: Lubalin, Burns and Rondthaler license phototype faces, spreading expressive display type.

events.label: Federal Design Improvement Program
events.note: After Nixon's memo, the NEA brings modernist identity and graphics standards to US federal agencies.

events.label: Vignelli New York City Subway diagram
events.note: Diagram over geography becomes the defining argument in transit cartography.

events.label: IBM eight-bar logo
events.note: Rand's striped revision becomes one of the most recognised corporate marks.

events.label: Pentagram founded
events.note: A partnership of equal designer-owners becomes a new model for the design firm.

events.label: AIGA/DOT Symbol Signs
events.note: 34 public pictograms set the standard for US wayfinding.

events.label: NASA worm logotype
events.note: Danne & Blackburn's mark, under the federal program, is the high point of public-sector modernism.

events.label: I♥NY
events.note: Milton Glaser's rebus shows a mark can change how people feel about a place.

events.label: National Park Service Unigrid
events.note: Vignelli's grid standardises every US national park brochure.

events.label: Pentagram opens in New York
events.note: Carries London wit into American identity design; later home of Scher and Bierut.
